title: Production Data Stack
body: When a number looks wrong at ADW — low utilization, a crusher stoppage, a drilling miss — the knee-jerk move is to argue about the headline figure. That's wasted time if you haven't checked which layer of the data actually broke.
keyPoints: Four workbooks measure the same day from different depths: running-hours log (raw meter/diesel), A&U (productive vs standby split), daily report (KPI summary), INX-SUM survey (independent ground-truth check). Each layer strips out something the one below kept.

The running-hours log total should sit 80–150 machine-hours above A&U operating hours per day — that's meal, prayer, and refuel time being reclassified out, not noise. If the gap is way off that range, something's miscoded before you even look at ratios.

A high truck count with a low survey number doesn't mean the fleet underperformed — it usually means loading happened outside the survey calculation area. Check loading position before you blame production.

When investigating a flagged number, read down the stack in order: daily report (what/when) → A&U (which unit, which reason column) → running-hours log (raw hours, diesel, operator Emp. No) → INX-SUM (ground-truth check if the total looks off).
Diesel burn out of ratio with running hours in the hours log is an early fault signal — it shows up there before it ever becomes a breakdown reason in A&U.
apply: If a unit's utilization looks low in the morning numbers, don't stop at the A&U percentage — pull the reason column and cross-check it against the running-hours log before you raise it in the client meeting.
